subject: Multi-species, multi-site density estimates, accounting for effort

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Multi-species, multi-site density estimates, accounting for effort
parts:
Hi,

I am learning how to use the Distance package in R, having for many years used Distance for Windows.

The kind of analysis I am trying to do involves generating separate density estimates for each species at each point count location. I want to do this in order to be able to carry out multivariate analyses to assess similarity in species assemblages between points. It doesn't matter to me that reliability in individual point estimates will be low - the overall patterns (in terms of how points cluster in ordination space in relation to variables such as habitat) are still useful.

I have attached an example dataset comprising 921 observations of 91 species detected at 79 points. The maximum distance within which birds were recorded was 100m. I am ignoring the influence of habitat on location, for the moment, but have assigned each species to one of 13 'detection groups'. Members of each group are assumed to be similarly detectable to one another. With the exception of one group (Hirundines and Swifts, DG13, with only 14 observations) all groups are more or less large enough to based a detection function on the distribution of detection distances.

My first question is whether I could or should use detection group as a co-variate, or whether I should more simply (but also more faffily) apply the ds function separately on each detection group, simply subsetting the whole dataset by detection group? The latter approach is equivalent to the one I have taken previously using the Distance programme. As far as I can see, applying ds separately, without co-variates, to each group has two possible benefits. Firstly, some of the error messages my tests have generated suggest that analyses without co-variates are a little more robust and less inclined to generate errors and warnings. Secondly, if detection distance distributions vary sufficiently between different groups of birds, this may justify applying different key and adjustment functions to model detectability in different detection groups. I'm not sure if this would be possible using a co-variate approach.

My second question relates to generating estimates for each species, at each point. In the Windows programme, I used to create a variable by concatenating (or pasting) species and site names in the following form "Species_Site", and then assigning this variable as a stratum, and specifying stratum as the appropriate level of resolution for density estimates in the Model Definition dialogue. However, the closest I have found to this in the ds function is the Region.Label variable. Is it possible to use this in a similar way? 

Finally, my last question is about how to ensure that densities are calculated correctly, taking into account all points where a species wasn't seen, as well as those points where it was. Am I right in thinking that, if I population the Region.Label variable with "Species_Site" (where Site=Point), then I should ensure that a 'blank' entry for every possible unique combination of Species and Site should be included in the dataset to which ds is applied? With 91 species and 79 points, the number of possible unique species-points combinations is 7189. So far, I haven't been able to take this approach successfully. If, as I have read in other posts is the correct approach, I set the distance variable to NA for these records (as in the code below), then I get an error message saying "Error in create.bins(data, cutpoints) : Some distances are NA, can't create bins."

Many thanks for any help you can give!

Best wishes,

Mark



EXAMPLE CODE

Data_OK<-read.csv("Amurum_birds.csv")

#Create Region.Label variable for observations, as concatentation of Species and Site
Data_OK$Region.Label <- paste(Data_OK$Species,Data_OK$Sample.Label,sep="_")

#Create points-habitat lookup table
Pt_table<-data.frame(matrix(ncol=2,nrow=length(Points)))
names(Pt_table)<-c("Point","Habitat")
Pt_table$Point<-Points
Pt_table$Habitat<-Data_OK[match(Pt_table$Point,Data_OK$Sample.Label),6]

#Create bird-DG table
Sp_table<-data.frame(aggregate(as.numeric(DG)~Species,Data_OK,mean))

#Set up 'blanks' file, with one blank for each possible value of Region.Label
Species <- as.character(unique(Data_OK$Species))
Points <- as.character(unique(Data_OK$Sample.Label))
Point_rep <- rep(Points,91)
SpeciesPt_rep <- rep(Species,each=79)
Est_rep <- paste(SpeciesHab_rep,Point_rep,sep="_")

Names_data<-names(Data_OK)
Blanks<-data.frame(matrix(nrow=length(Est_rep), ncol=length(Names_data)))
names(Blanks)<-Names_data
Blanks$Region.Label<-Est_rep
Blanks$Species<-Species_rep
Blanks$Sample.Label<-Point_rep
Blanks$size<-rep("",nrow(Blanks))
Blanks$DG<-Sp_table[match(Blanks$Species,Sp_table$Species),2]
Blanks$Habitat<-Pt_table[match(Blanks$Sample.Label,Pt_table$Point),2]
Blanks$observer<-rep(1,nrow(Blanks))
Blanks$distance<-rep(NA,nrow(Blanks))
Blanks$Effort<-rep(1,nrow(Blanks))

Blanks$DG<-as.factor(Blanks$DG)
Data_OK$DG<-as.factor(Data_OK$DG)
Data_and_blanks<-rbind(Data_OK,Blanks)

#Run model
dist.bins<-c(0,20,40,60,100)
Model <- ds(Data_and_blanks,transect="point",adjustment="herm",formula=~as.factor(DG),cutpoints=dist.bins)
plot(Model)
ds.gof(Model,cutpoints=dist.bins,nc=5)
SumMod<-summary(Model)

write.csv(SumMod$dht$individuals$D,"Amurum_distance_output.csv",row.names = F)

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Multi-species, multi-site density estimates, accounting for effort
parts:
Mark

I've done a bit of fiddling with your data on a wet Sunday afternoon.  I have some partial answers to some of your questions.

To get my head around the data, I read them in and fabricated values for "Region.Label" and "Area" -- required to get abundance/density estimates calculated.  I also wanted a quick look at the data.

birds <- read.csv("C:/Users/erexs/Downloads/Amurum_birds.csv")
birds$Area <- 1000              # fabricated
birds$Region.Label <- "full"    # fabricated
table(birds$Sample.Label, birds$DG)
all.species <- ds(birds, transect = "point")
mrds:::plot.ds(all.species$ddf,  pdf=TRUE, main="All data combined")
all.species$dht$individuals$Nhat.by.sample

The plot of the PDF shows lots of heaping to favoured distances (perhaps ending in "0") in the data

I've not printed the `all.species$dht$individuals$Nhat.by.sample` but that provides point-specific abundance estimates.  Proceeding to get "assemblage-specific" estimates:

group5 <- ds(birds[birds$DG=="D5", ], transect="point")
mrds:::plot.ds(group5$ddf,  pdf=TRUE, main="D5")
group5$dht$individuals$Nhat.by.sample

shows something a bit better behaved

As to your questions: 

detection group as a covariate:  that is a model-selection problem.  Fit models separately by group or with group as a covariate; perform AIC comparison.  However, as you note, you may want different key functions between groups, which would be hard to accomplish with group as covariate.

point-specific estimates: using the "Nhat.by.sample" component of the fitted object as shown above.  But to get the 'dht' component of the fitted object requires specification of "Region.Label" and "Area" in the data.

adjusting effort for points without detections:  correct, you'll need NA for distances associated with species-point combinations without detections.  I think the bug associates with NA distances was corrected in Distance 0.9.4 (this from package news: Distance version 0.9.4 * Object ID uniqueness stopped abundance estimation from working (since NA IDs were "not unique")). Current version is 0.9.7--see if that doesn't solve that problem.

Let us know how you get on.

parts:
Hi Eric,

Thanks for fiddling (and getting back to me) so promptly - much appreciated!

Just to check that I understand your answers (in bold below, followed by my comments):
The plot of the PDF shows lots of heaping to favoured distances (perhaps ending in "0") in the data

I had seen this heaping and in my code specify cutpoints as follows:
dist.bins<-c(0,20,40,60,100)
...cutpoints=dist.bins
I think that should fix it (my histograms with these cutpoints look pretty reasonable).

detection group as a covariate:  that is a model-selection problem.  Fit models separately by group or with group as a covariate; perform AIC comparison.  However, as you note, you may want different key functions between groups, which would be hard to accomplish with group as covariate.

Great, thanks for that. I think it probably makes sense to subset by group and fit the models separately (I saw the code you included in your reply to Mauro that allows automated selection between three key functions using AIC. I will try and incorporate this into my script).

point-specific estimates: using the "Nhat.by.sample" component of the fitted object as shown above.  But to get the 'dht' component of the fitted object requires specification of "Region.Label" and "Area" in the data.
Just to make sure I understand this - Region.Label should specify both point count location (Sample.Label) and species (e.g. ADTDO_1)?

adjusting effort for points without detections:  correct, you'll need NA for distances associated with species-point combinations without detections.  I think the bug associates with NA distances was corrected in Distance 0.9.4 (this from package news: Distance version 0.9.4 * Object ID uniqueness stopped abundance estimation from working (since NA IDs were "not unique")). Current version is 0.9.7--see if that doesn't solve that problem.

Again - thanks. I had seen this problem referred to before my Distance users, but wasn't aware that the relevant bug had been fixed in the latest versions. I have downloaded and installed version 0.9.7 (had to install up to date version of mrds first), so hopefully that will forestall further objections to NA values for distances.

Best wishes!

Mark
